notation.meaning: Marginal utility of consumption in period $t$
Capital left after the last period of a finite horizon
Last period of a finite horizon

blocks.md: If the world ends next year, there is no point keeping machines past that date: anything left over should have been eaten. With no end date, that rule cannot be applied directly, because there is no last year. The transversality condition is its stand-in. It says that, looking far enough ahead, the value of the capital you are still holding, weighted by how little you care about the distant future, has to shrink to nothing. A plan that keeps piling up capital forever without ever consuming it breaks this rule.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: The Euler equation and the resource constraint alone allow many paths; this condition picks the optimal one.
For the problem $\max\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\beta^tU(c_t)$ subject to $c_t + k_{t+1} = f(k_t) + (1-\delta)k_t$:
$\beta^tU'(c_t)$ is the value, in today's utility, of one unit of output in period $t$, so the product is the present value of the capital carried out of period $t$.

With a last period $T$, and capital convertible one-for-one into consumption, the optimum has $k_{T+1} = 0$: leftover capital could have been consumed. Letting $T \to \infty$, the condition $\beta^TU'(c_T)k_{T+1} = 0$ becomes the limit above.

In a steady state $U'(c_t) = U'(\bar{c})$ and $k_{t+1} = \bar{k}$ are constant, so $\beta^tU'(\bar{c})\bar{k} \to 0$ whenever $\beta < 1$: the steady state satisfies the condition. With $\beta = 1$ it would not, which is one reason the golden rule appears only as a limiting case of the Ramsey model.

- **Writing it without "= 0"** (or as a limit of $k_t$ alone). Capital need not go to zero; only its discounted value does.
- **Treating it as optional.** Without it, paths that satisfy every Euler equation but over-accumulate capital look optimal.

- Macroeconomics: every infinite-horizon growth and business cycle model ([Ramsey-Cass-Koopmans Model](note:ramsey-cass-koopmans-model)).
- Finance: ruling out bubbles and Ponzi schemes (the no-Ponzi condition is its budget-side cousin).
